newsitem.title: UK: Nadir tells lawyers to open abuse case against SFO.
newsitem.headline: Nadir tells lawyers to open abuse case against SFO.

text.p: Fugitive Turkish Cypriot tycoon Asil Nadir has told his lawyers to sue Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) for wrongly trying to prosecute him for fraud, ITV independent television said on Tuesday.

Nadir told ITV it was unlikely he would return to Britain in the forseeable future. In the past, he had hinted he could well return after the Conservative government had lost power, as it did in a May 1 election.
ITV showed Nadir -- who fled to North Cyprus four years ago while on bail ahead of a fraud trial -- signing a letter to his lawyers instructing them to sue the SFO for abusing its legal power.

ITV interviewed two people -- a police informer and a former timeshare saleswoman -- who said they had taken part in an SFO conspiracy intended to make it look as though Nadir was trying to bribe the trial judge.
The programme also said the SFO officer in charge of the Nadir file had been disciplined and penalised for how she had handled the case.
An SFO spokesman declined to comment on the report, saying it still wanted to put Nadir on trial.
"We intend to proceed against him when he returns or is returned to the United Kingdom," he said by telephone.
Nadir fled Britain in May 1993 while awaiting trial on theft and false accounting charges following the collapse of his London-based Polly Peck fruits to electronics empire.
Nadir cannot be extradited from North Cyprus -- which is not recognised by the UK -- and made it clear he would not be returning to Britain in the forseeable future.
"I would love to come back to Britain because I love the country, I've spent the bulk of my life in the UK and I love its people," he told ITV.
"My grievance is with the wrongdoers and to expect me to come today to Britain, to the unknown, I think would be rather naive," he said.

Michael Francis, who said he was a former police informer, claimed he had been used by the British police in a bid to trap Nadir by suggesting to him that he could avoid a trial by paying the judge a large bribe.

"I was supposed to contact Asil Nadir and put a proposition to him that if were to pay 3.5 million pounds ($5.7 million), he would be given back his passport...and that the charges against him would be greatly reduced and eventually the charges would be dropped," he told ITV.
Preparations for the trial were plunged into chaos when the authorities said they had discovered an attempt to pervert the course of justice. The charges were later found to be groundless.

Former timeshare saleswoman Wendy Welsher, who said she also took part in the alleged attempt to smear Nadir, told ITV she had fled to North Cyprus after unnamed British officials had threatened her life.
